title: Cabral's Factory and the Miri Fire

title_i18n.en: Cabral's Factory and the Miri Fire

subtitle: Trade, Fire and the Birth of a Sea War
figure: Pedro Alvares Cabral and Vasco da Gama
region: Calicut harbor and the Arabian Sea
moral: When commerce chooses terror, trust burns with the ships.

sources.citation: Anonymous Portuguese accounts of Cabral's voyage; João de Barros, Da Asia
sources.note: Portuguese evidence for the factory conflict and reprisals at Calicut.
Detailed Portuguese narrative of da Gama's 1502 seizure and burning of the Miri.

sources.citation: Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Career and Legend of Vasco da Gama (1997); M.N. Pearson, The Portuguese in India (1987)
sources.note: Modern scholarship on Portuguese coercion, trade and violence.

panels.shot: epic wide of a stormy Calicut harbor, one Portuguese ship firing while another Indian vessel burns in the distance

dialogue.text: In 1500–1502, Pedro Álvares Cabral and Vasco da Gama turned Calicut’s trading coast into a battlefield, where a factory riot and a burning pilgrim ship began a brutal war for the Indian Ocean.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a map table in a dim cabin, Indian Ocean routes marked in ink

dialogue.text: After Vasco da Gama’s first voyage, the Portuguese Crown sent Pedro Álvares Cabral in 1500 to make Calicut a gateway to a spice monopoly, backed not just by gold, but by guns.

panels.shot: wide harbor view as Cabral’s fleet anchors off Calicut, bustling local craft around

dialogue.text: Calicut, ruled by the Zamorin, was a free port where Arab, Indian and other merchants shared the pepper trade. The Portuguese wanted privileged access, lower prices and tighter control.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a newly established factory, bales of pepper stacked, tense faces

dialogue.text: A factory was set up in Calicut. But disputes over prices, customs dues and rival merchants quickly sharpened. Each side accused the other of cheating, each felt the other was arrogant.

panels.shot: tight, tense interior with shouting figures, Portuguese guards gripping weapons

dialogue.text: Portuguese accounts describe an attack on the factory after these quarrels escalated, with many of their men killed. The details are murky, but the break with Calicut was sudden and bloody.

panels.shot: low-angle view from the shore as Cabral’s ships unleash cannon fire toward Calicut

dialogue.text: Cabral answered with bombardment. Portuguese sources say his ships shelled Calicut’s shore and seized or burned Indian vessels, turning a trade quarrel into open, punitive war.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye over the sea as mixed Indian shipping scatters from Portuguese warships

dialogue.text: Ships belonging to Calicut-linked traders were targeted. The message was clear: resistance to Portuguese demands could be met not with negotiation, but with destruction at sea.

panels.shot: medium shot of Cabral meeting Cochin’s ruler in a coastal courtyard

dialogue.text: After breaking with Calicut, Cabral moved toward Cochin and other rival ports. Portuguese sources describe new alliances there, binding their guns to local enemies of the Zamorin’s city.

panels.shot: transition shot: parchment letter bearing the royal Portuguese seal being signed

dialogue.text: Lisbon watched. Cabral’s clash with Calicut hardened attitudes. By the time Vasco da Gama sailed again in 1502, Portuguese policy mixed commerce, crusading language and deliberate terror.

panels.shot: wide ocean shot as da Gama’s fleet meets the large pilgrim ship Miri

dialogue.text: In 1502, Gaspar Correia’s account says, da Gama encountered the Miri, a great ship carrying Muslim pilgrims and valuable cargo, bound from India toward the Red Sea and beyond.

panels.shot: medium shot across the water: da Gama shouting from his deck toward the Miri

dialogue.speaker: pedro_alvares_cabral_and_vasco_da_gama
dialogue.text: The king’s justice reaches these seas. You will pay, or be an example.

panels.shot: closer shot of the Miri’s deck with kneeling figures and chests of goods displayed

dialogue.text: Correia’s narrative describes ransom talks and pleas for mercy. The ship’s people offered goods and wealth, hoping to buy safety for their vessel and those crowded upon it.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle from the Miri’s deck, ropes and flames beginning along her side

dialogue.text: Portuguese sources, including Correia, say that when these negotiations failed, da Gama had the Miri seized and set alight, using it as a public act of terror on the open sea.

panels.shot: wide, distant shot of the Miri burning, other ships watching from afar

dialogue.text: Correia’s account speaks of hundreds aboard—perhaps two to four hundred—trapped on the burning pilgrim ship. The numbers differ in sources, but all agree the human loss was immense.

panels.shot: close-up on da Gama’s face lit by firelight reflection, expression cold and resolved

dialogue.text: Modern historians note that religious language sharpened da Gama’s actions, but behind it lay a goal: to frighten Muslim and Indian merchants, and reshape Indian Ocean trade by force.

panels.shot: shoreline shot back at Calicut, angry crowds and mariners gesturing to the sea

dialogue.text: News of Cabral’s bombardment and da Gama’s burning of the Miri spread. For Calicut’s merchants and rulers, these acts marked the Portuguese as traders who wielded terror, not trust.

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot: Portuguese ships near Cochin, Calicut’s harbor bristling with local fleets

dialogue.text: From this moment, alliances hardened. The Portuguese drew closer to Cochin and other rivals, while Calicut and its seafaring captains began to see the ocean itself as a new front in war.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle of a Malabari war captain on a deck, Portuguese ship distant

dialogue.text: In the years ahead, figures like the Kunjali Marakkars would rise from this coast, answering cannon with counter-raids, as trade routes between India and the world turned into contested battle-lines.

panels.shot: final contemplative shot: charred driftwood from a ship on a quiet beach at sunset

dialogue.text: Cabral’s ruined factory and the burning of the Miri show how, when commerce chooses terror, every ship becomes a battlefield and every harbor remembers that trust can be lost in a single fire.
